mcqs.question: You define `class Car { String make; void drive() {} }` but never call `new Car()`. How much memory has been allocated for Car objects at this point?
options: Zero — the class definition only describes the shape; memory for an object is allocated when `new` runs
Enough for one Car object, created automatically the moment the class is loaded
Enough for one Car object per thread that references the class
It depends only on the size of the compiled `drive` method's bytecode
mcqs.explanation: A class is a compiled description, not a stamped-out object — no instance memory exists until `new` runs. The tempting wrong answer confuses loading a class definition with instantiating an object; loading just makes the blueprint available, it doesn't create a Car.

mcqs.question: Given `class Counter { int count = 10; Counter() { count = 20; } }`, what is `count` immediately after `new Counter()`?
options: 10 — the constructor never actually executes because field initializers take precedence
0 — uninitialized fields default to zero and the field initializer is ignored
20 — the field initializer runs first, then the constructor body runs and overwrites it
Undefined — most languages leave this ordering unspecified
mcqs.explanation: Field initializers run before the constructor body, in declaration order, so `count` is set to 10 and then the constructor body sets it to 20. This ordering is specified and predictable in Java, C++, C#, and similar languages — it isn't left to chance.

mcqs.question: Variables `a` and `b` both hold a reference to the same `Car` object. What happens when you run `a.mileage += 100`?
options: `b.mileage` is unaffected, because assignment always copies the underlying object
`b.mileage` reflects the change too, because `a` and `b` point at the same object in memory
A new Car object is silently created for `a`, leaving `b`'s Car unchanged
It throws a runtime error, because two references can't legally point at one object
mcqs.explanation: A reference variable holds an address, not the object itself, so `a` and `b` pointing at the same object means a mutation through either one is visible through both. Two references sharing one object is completely legal and is the default behavior for object assignment.

mcqs.question: A class declares `static List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();`, intending it to be each object's own per-instance tag list. What actually happens at runtime?
options: Each new object automatically gets its own independent copy of the list
The list is recreated fresh every time any method on any instance is called
Only the first-created object can modify the list; later objects see a read-only copy
Every instance shares the exact same list, so a mutation through one object is visible through all others
mcqs.explanation: `static` means the field belongs to the class, not to any instance, so there is exactly one list shared by every object — the opposite of a per-instance default. Per-object defaults must be instance fields, typically initialized in the constructor.
